content: The follicular phase, also known as the proliferative phase, is a stage in the menstrual cycle (or estrous cycle in other mammals) during which ovarian follicles mature. This phase concludes with ovulation and is primarily regulated by the hormone estradiol. Follicle Recruitment Follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), secreted by the anterior pituitary gland, begins to rise during the final days of the preceding menstrual cycle. FSH levels peak and are most critical during the first week of the follicular phase. This increase in FSH recruits five to seven tertiary-stage ovarian follicles, also referred to as Graafian or antral follicles, into the menstrual cycle. These follicles have been developing over the course of approximately a year through a process called folliculogenesis. The recruited follicles compete for dominance. FSH stimulates the proliferation of granulosa cells within the developing follicles and promotes the expression of luteinizing hormone (LH) receptors on these granulosa cells. Under the influence of FSH, aromatase and p450 enzymes are activated, leading to the production of estrogen by the granulosa cells. The rising estrogen levels stimulate the release of gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH), which in turn increases LH production. LH plays a critical role by inducing androgen synthesis in the thecal cells, promoting the proliferation, differentiation, and secretory activity of the thecal cells, and further increasing LH receptor expression on granulosa cells. Estrogen Surge Approximately two to three days after LH levels begin to rise, one follicle (or occasionally two) emerges as the dominant follicle. It is widely believed that the dominant follicle produces sufficient estrogen to suppress GnRH secretion, which subsequently reduces LH and FSH levels. This decline in LH and FSH causes the majority of the recruited follicles to undergo atresia (degeneration), while the dominant follicle continues to mature. Estrogen levels continue to rise for several days, typically around six days on average, though this duration can vary. Elevated estrogen levels stimulate the formation of a new layer of endometrium in the uterus, known histologically as the proliferative endometrium. Additionally, cervical crypts are stimulated to produce fertile cervical mucus, which reduces vaginal acidity and creates a more favorable environment for sperm. This mucus also has a specific texture that facilitates sperm movement through the cervix and toward the fallopian tubes, where they await ovulation. High estrogen levels may also cause a slight decrease in basal body temperature. LH Surge and Ovulation Estrogen levels reach their peak just before the onset of the LH surge. A temporary drop in steroid hormone levels between the start of the LH surge and ovulation may result in mid-cycle spotting or bleeding. The preovulatory LH surge triggers the first meiotic division in the oocyte and initiates the luteinization of thecal and granulosa cells. Ovulation typically occurs approximately 30 hours (± 2 hours) after the onset of the LH surge, which is when LH first becomes detectable in urine. Follicular Waves The interval from the recruitment of tertiary-stage follicles to ovulation generally spans about two weeks, corresponding to days 1–14 of an idealized 28-day menstrual cycle. However, the follicular phase can sometimes extend significantly longer if no dominant follicle is selected. In such cases, additional tertiary-stage follicles are recruited, and the process restarts. A study of women with regular menstrual cycles found that none ovulated after the first wave of follicle development. Instead, 68% of cycles resulted in ovulation after the second wave, while 32% ovulated after the third wave. Fertility awareness methods may describe these multiple waves of follicular development as a split peak, referring to the characteristic changes in cervical mucus patterns that can occur.
